summary.text: Collision theory is a principle of chemistry used to predict the rates of chemical reactions.
It says only some collisions succeed: the particles must hit with the correct orientation and with enough energy, called activation energy, to break old bonds and form new ones.
Higher concentration, higher temperature or a catalyst each lead to more successful collisions, so the reaction rate goes up.

facts.label: Proposed by
facts.value: Max Trautz in 1916, William Lewis in 1918

facts.label: A successful collision needs
facts.value: The correct orientation and enough energy

facts.label: Weak spot
facts.value: Rate constants are often estimated incorrectly

facts.label: Orientation example
facts.value: Few H₂ and ethylene collisions approach the bonding zone

items.prompt: Two molecules hit each other at high speed, but with the wrong orientation. What does collision theory say?

options.label: The collision still succeeds, since speed alone breaks any bond
The collision may well fail to react, because correct orientation is needed as well as energy
The collision succeeds, because every hard hit counts as successful
The collision succeeds, but only if a catalyst is also present

items.explain: Only some collisions are successful: the particles must hit with the correct orientation and with enough energy.

items.prompt: A chemist squeezes twice as many reactant particles into the same flask. What does collision theory predict?

options.label: More collisions happen, and so more successful collisions
Fewer successful collisions, because the particles get in each other's way
The same number of successful collisions, since energy per collision is unchanged
Fewer collisions, since crowding slows the particles down

items.explain: Increasing the concentration of reactant brings about more collisions and hence more successful collisions.

items.prompt: A cook turns up the heat under a reaction. In collision theory terms, what does the heat mainly do?

options.label: It lowers the activation energy for every collision
It turns every collision into one with the correct orientation
It raises the average energy of the molecules, so more collisions carry enough energy
It makes the molecules larger, so they collide more often

items.explain: Raising the temperature increases the average kinetic energy of the molecules, which increases the number of collisions that have enough energy.

items.prompt: A catalyst is added to a mixture of reactants. How does collision theory say it speeds the reaction up?

options.label: It forces the molecules to collide twice as often
It raises the energy of each molecule so every hit works
It stops molecules from colliding in the wrong orientation
Less energy is needed for the change, so more collisions have enough of it

items.explain: When a catalyst is involved in the collision, less energy is required for the chemical change, so more collisions have sufficient energy.

items.prompt: Predicted rate constants from collision theory often miss the real values, and miss by more for bigger molecules. Which assumption is mostly to blame?

options.label: That molecules in a gas collide at all
That the particles are spheres able to react from every direction
That reactions need any energy to get going
That temperature has any effect on the rate

items.explain: The theory supposes particles are spherical and can react in all directions, but the orientation of collisions is not always proper, and more complex molecules suffer more.

items.prompt: Reactant molecules are dissolved in a liquid, not floating freely as a gas. What controls how often they collide?

options.label: Their spreading by diffusion and Brownian motion
Only how hard the liquid is stirred
Only the pull of gravity on the liquid
The shape of the container alone

items.explain: In solutions, the collision frequency of the solute molecules is controlled by diffusion or Brownian motion of individual molecules.
